data.title: Nvidia reportedly limits Chinese access to overseas AI cloud services
data.description:
Nvidia has reportedly asked its cloud computing partners to reduce their business with Chinese customers, directing them to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, the instructions were issued in recent months, citing five people familiar with the matter. They were communicated verbally through Nvidia’s sales staff and regional teams rather than through formal written policies, and apply only to future contracts. Existing agreements remain unaffected.

The Information separately reported that the guidance is not mandatory and has not been strictly enforced. The publication also said Nvidia was encouraging cloud providers, including Nvidia-backed neocloud operators, to diversify their customer base and identify the end users accessing its chips.

Nvidia has not publicly explained how the reported 51% requirement would be calculated or monitored.

US export controls address overseas GPU access

The reported instructions come amid US restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductors used in AI development. Since 2022, Washington has introduced export controls limiting shipments of certain Nvidia processors to China.

Chinese technology companies have also accessed advanced computing resources through overseas cloud providers, allowing them to rent GPU capacity without importing the hardware. These arrangements provide access to Nvidia-powered infrastructure for AI workloads, including model training.

In May 2025, the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a policy statement identifying circumstances in which exports or transfers of advanced computing chips to foreign infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) providers could require an export licence.

Under the guidance, licensing requirements can apply when exporters know that hardware supplied to foreign cloud providers will be used to train AI models for or on behalf of entities headquartered in China or other designated countries of concern, where the activity involves weapons of mass destruction or military-intelligence end uses or end users. The policy addresses specific activities rather than imposing a blanket prohibition on Chinese companies accessing overseas cloud services.

Separate BIS guidance issued in May 2025 recommended that semiconductor suppliers verify customer identities, ownership structures, and the intended use of advanced computing hardware. It also identified data centre inspections, end-user certifications, and independent audits as measures to prevent chips from reaching restricted entities.

BIS also recommended additional scrutiny of data centres with infrastructure capable of operating servers containing advanced computing chips at more than 10 megawatts. The agency said facilities at this scale can provide access to large amounts of computing capacity for AI model training.

US officials have also examined Chinese AI companies’ access to Nvidia chips through overseas data centres. One reported case involved Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi AI model, following allegations that the company had used Nvidia processors housed outside China.

Nvidia tightens checks on Asian cloud providers

Nvidia had previously tightened its screening of Asian customers. In July, the Financial Times reported that the company had removed more than half of its previously approved Asian buyers from a list of companies authorised to purchase its AI chips, with smaller GPU cloud providers among those affected.

The stricter compliance checks were intended to prevent advanced US semiconductors from reaching China through third countries. According to the report, Nvidia increased its due diligence procedures in Singapore, Malaysia, and Japan, including visits to customer data centres, contract verification, and interviews with end users.

Companies that failed the initial reviews were reportedly removed from the approved customer list but could reapply after addressing compliance deficiencies.

The reported 51% requirement has raised concerns among cloud providers operating Nvidia-powered infrastructure. According to the Financial Times, some operators have warned that securing enough non-Chinese customers would be difficult, particularly outside the US.

A Singapore-based cloud provider told the publication that strict enforcement would hurt its business. Other operators reportedly warned that they might have to reduce operations if they could not attract enough customers outside China.

Some overseas data centre operators have also begun seeking additional non-Chinese customers in response to the reported instructions, according to the Financial Times.

Nvidia has not publicly confirmed or denied the reported customer allocation requirement. In a statement provided to AFP, the company addressed the role of US computing infrastructure in the global AI market.

“Data centres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide,” Nvidia said.

The company added that longstanding US policy encourages cloud providers to build on American infrastructure and seek customers internationally.

(Photo by Brecht Corbeel)

data.title: Microsoft 365 outage caused by software bug introduced in July
data.description:
Microsoft has traced a nearly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage on November 12 to a software defect introduced in July. The incident disrupted Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services after a failure spread across the company’s networking gateway infrastructure.

In a preliminary post-incident report dated November 15, Microsoft identified three contributing factors: a software defect dating back to July, increased load on the affected networking gateway following a Microsoft Teams failover, and reduced server capacity.

The disruption began at 4:20 p.m. UTC on November 12 and continued until 4:10 p.m. UTC the following day. Exchange Online was the most affected service, with Microsoft reporting that most users were unable to access their mailboxes through Outlook or other email clients. Email delivery was also delayed for many customers.

Other affected services included Microsoft Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, OneDrive, Defender, and Purview. Microsoft said most of these services remained largely accessible, although features dependent on Exchange Online experienced disruptions.

What caused the Microsoft 365 outage?

According to Microsoft, the software defect originated from an update developed specifically for its Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. The update began rolling out in July and was deployed globally over several weeks without any reported problems.

The defect involved competing operations within an internal Windows process, known as lock contention, which caused servers to exhaust their CPU and memory resources under certain workloads. Microsoft said the issue was specific to its networking gateway infrastructure and did not affect broader Windows deployments.

Microsoft’s standard load testing failed to identify the defect because its test environments used different traffic patterns and hardware configurations. According to the company, testing primarily relied on less powerful machines with fewer CPU cores, while the defect became more pronounced on newer servers with higher core counts.

The problem surfaced after Microsoft Teams traffic was redirected from an alternative networking gateway to the primary gateway supporting Exchange Online. The failover occurred approximately 15 hours before the outage, increasing the load on the shared infrastructure.

Around 14% of gateway server capacity was unavailable because of an unrelated issue. Microsoft said the reduced capacity alone was insufficient to cause an outage, but the Teams failover increased pressure on the remaining servers, triggering the existing defect.

Following the Teams failover, load on the affected gateway increased gradually, and isolated server failures began appearing in some regions. Microsoft’s automated systems initially attempted to address these failures before connectivity problems became more widespread.

Why the failure spread globally

As affected servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s automated traffic management systems redirected connections to other operational servers. This increased pressure on the remaining infrastructure, causing the same defect to spread through the gateway fleet.

“At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive,” Microsoft said in its preliminary report. The cascading failure developed in less than two hours as traffic was redistributed across fewer available servers.

Microsoft later determined that the elevated server load was not caused by an overall increase in traffic. Instead, the growing number of unavailable servers placed additional pressure on the remaining infrastructure.

Microsoft’s networking gateway infrastructure consists of thousands of capacity units distributed across multiple regions. Although the infrastructure includes mechanisms designed to isolate failures between partitions, Microsoft said a separate issue prevented those safeguards from containing the disruption. The preliminary report did not explain the underlying cause of that issue.

Microsoft operates two independent network gateway systems that allow services to switch between infrastructure during disruptions. Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office applications were able to move away from the affected gateway, allowing some functionality to recover earlier.

Exchange Online could not switch to the alternative gateway because of scaling limitations, according to Microsoft. Consequently, mailbox access remained disrupted while other Microsoft 365 services began recovering.

How Microsoft restored its services

Microsoft’s automated recovery systems were unable to restore services because they were not designed to handle such a widespread infrastructure failure. Servers that restarted were quickly overwhelmed by accumulated connection requests and became unresponsive again.

Recovery was further complicated by the age of the software defect. Because the update had been deployed several months earlier, Microsoft’s standard rollback mechanisms and feature controls could not quickly reverse the change.

Engineers attempted to restore affected servers and redistribute traffic, but these measures did not produce sustained recovery. Microsoft subsequently disabled some automated traffic redirection mechanisms and adjusted service load to reduce pressure on the affected infrastructure.

After identifying the defect, Microsoft developed an update to restore the affected connection-handling code to its previous working state. Engineers temporarily removed groups of servers from service, applied the update, and restarted them before gradually returning them to operation.

Microsoft began deploying the corrective update on November 13 and confirmed that the updated servers were stable before expanding deployment across its infrastructure. Recovery progressed throughout the day, with improvements in Asia-Pacific and Europe as affected systems returned to service.

Global webmail availability returned to expected levels by 2:17 p.m. UTC on November 13. Microsoft confirmed that customers were no longer experiencing active disruptions by 4:10 p.m. UTC, although monitoring and processing of delayed email continued afterward.

Following the outage, Microsoft increased infrastructure capacity and introduced additional monitoring for connection-handling problems and traffic redirection. The company also implemented controls intended to prevent traffic redistribution from causing similar cascading failures.

Microsoft extended its email delivery window to prevent delayed messages from being returned as undeliverable. According to the company, messages queued during the incident were subsequently processed.

Microsoft said these immediate corrective measures had been completed. A more comprehensive list of repair measures is scheduled for publication in its final post-incident report on November 20.

data.title: OVHcloud launches 55 cloud and AI products amid Europe’s sovereignty push
data.description:
French cloud provider OVHcloud has announced 55 new cloud computing and AI products, covering computing infrastructure, AI development, networking, and enterprise applications.

The products were unveiled at the OVHcloud AI Summit on November 19, 2026, as the company expands its European-hosted cloud services. The announcement includes plans for new AI hardware, application development tools, and security capabilities.

According to Synergy Research Group, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google accounted for a combined 70% of Europe’s cloud infrastructure services market in July 2025, while European providers held approximately 15%. The regional market generated €61 billion in revenue in 2024, having expanded sixfold since 2017.

Europe’s push for cloud sovereignty

In April 2026, the European Commission awarded four contracts allowing EU institutions, bodies, and agencies to procure sovereign cloud services worth up to €180 million over six years. The procurement aims to diversify suppliers and reduce dependence on a single provider.

OVHcloud was among the selected providers through a consortium led by Luxembourg’s Post Telecom, alongside Clever Cloud. Other successful bidders included Germany’s STACKIT, France’s Scaleway, and a consortium led by Belgium’s Proximus.

The Commission’s Cloud Sovereignty Framework assesses providers across criteria covering legal jurisdiction, data and AI control, operational independence, and supply chain transparency. The consortium involving OVHcloud achieved SEAL-3, a classification that addresses digital resilience, including protection against supply chain disruptions involving non-EU third parties.

The framework also distinguishes between data sovereignty and technological autonomy, as European data hosting does not necessarily eliminate reliance on foreign hardware or software suppliers.

The European Commission proposed the Cloud and AI Development Act in June 2026 to support cloud infrastructure investment, expand data centre capacity, and establish a common EU framework for assessing cloud and AI sovereignty.

Cloud dependence was also examined by the European Central Bank (ECB) in its November 2026 Financial Stability Review. The ECB estimated that AWS, Microsoft, and Google accounted for 82% of Europe’s broader cloud market in 2025, using a definition that also includes certain software-as-a-service activities.

The ECB identified operational risks associated with dependence on a small number of providers, including service outages, software changes, pricing adjustments, and application programming interface (API) restrictions. It also acknowledged that major cloud providers benefit from economies of scale and substantial cybersecurity resources.

Expanding cloud and AI infrastructure

OVHcloud announced plans to add Nvidia RTX 6000 Pro, Blackwell B300, and Rubin R200 GPUs to its Bare Metal and Public Cloud offerings.

According to OVHcloud, its data centres have sufficient capacity to accommodate up to 60,000 B300 GPUs or 35,000 R200 GPUs. These figures represent potential infrastructure capacity rather than the number of GPUs currently deployed.

The planned GPU offerings are intended to support AI model training and inference workloads. While OVHcloud operates European infrastructure, these services will continue to rely on processors supplied by US-based Nvidia.

OVHcloud is also expanding its Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networking services with web application firewalls, VPNs, private DNS, and load balancing capabilities. Other additions include Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) and BGP Service, allowing customers to retain existing IP address ranges and manage network routing.

OVHcloud Connect, its private network connectivity service, is available across 40 points of presence worldwide. The company also announced object storage performance improvements while maintaining its policy of including outbound data transfer in the service.

The infrastructure expansion includes AI Fabric, developed using technology from Blade.sh, which supports the deployment of Python-based environments for AI agents. OVHcloud also introduced Serverless Containers, Serverless Functions, and Messaging & Events services for running applications without directly managing the underlying servers.

Its AI Endpoints service is being expanded with approximately 100 additional models, including voice and image models. Through technology from Gladia, the service will support speech transcription and voice generation in more than 100 languages.

The new offerings span Public Cloud, single-tenant Private Cloud, and on-premises deployment models. OVHcloud also provides separately qualified cloud services for customers with specific security and data protection requirements.

Enterprise AI and European data control

Alongside its infrastructure announcements, OVHcloud introduced OVHai Workspace, an enterprise AI platform combining productivity applications, website management, and corporate information search.

The platform includes three areas: Productivity for workplace applications, Web AI for website creation and management, and Knowledge Platform for searching enterprise information.

An alpha version of the Productivity service is available free of charge with 5GB of storage per user. OVHcloud said the data is hosted in Europe and is not used to train AI models.

The Knowledge Platform combines semantic and keyword-based search to retrieve information from enterprise documents. According to OVHcloud, the search service supports collections containing hundreds of millions of documents and is designed for employees and AI agents.

OVHcloud also announced AI Agents, a service for deploying, managing, and monitoring AI agents connected to enterprise applications. The offering supports nearly 480 connectors and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

Additional security services include Cloud Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) for encryption key management, confidential computing for protecting data during processing, and application-specific distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) protection.

These announcements follow OVHcloud’s September 2026 confirmation that its SNC Cloud Platform had obtained SecNumCloud qualification from France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI. It became OVHcloud’s third qualified offering, following Bare Metal Pod and VMware on OVHcloud.

The qualification applies to the specified services rather than the company’s entire product portfolio. OVHcloud said it is preparing to expand SNC Cloud Platform beyond France, with Germany, Italy, and Poland among its planned European locations.

OVHcloud is also developing its own AI models. On November 17, the company announced Olala mini 7A1B, the first model in its Olala family of large language models.

The model was trained using three European public supercomputers: Jupiter, MeluXina, and Jean Zay. OVHcloud valued the computing resources provided for training at the equivalent of €7 million in compute time.

Olala mini uses a seven-billion-parameter architecture, with approximately one billion active parameters. It supports a context window of 32,000 tokens and is designed to operate on GPUs with as little as 8GB of memory.

OVHcloud said the model is being released under the Apache 2.0 licence, together with its weights, pretrained base model, technical report, and AI Act compliance documentation. The licence allows organisations to use, modify, and distribute the model subject to its terms.

French search engine Qwant has already adopted the model for its AI-generated search answers. OVHcloud reported that Qwant achieved 20% faster responses and reduced operating costs to one-third of those associated with its previous model.

OVHcloud expects version 1.1 to extend the model’s context window to 128,000 tokens by the end of 2026. Its longer-term development plans include models for enterprise AI agents, cloud operations, and cybersecurity, as well as models capable of running locally on user devices.

(Photo by Markus Spiske)

data.title: AWS launches cloud emulator built entirely by AI agents
data.description:
AWS has released an open-source cloud emulator developed entirely by autonomous AI agents, allowing developers to build and test applications locally without deploying resources to the cloud.

Called AWS Emulator, the tool supports AWS APIs and works with existing software development kits (SDKs), command-line tools, and AI coding agents. AWS said thousands of autonomous agents wrote the software without human code review.

The emulator is available at no additional service charge and does not require an AWS account for local testing. Its source code has also been published on GitHub under a Creative Commons CC0 licence.

Testing AWS applications locally

AWS Emulator allows developers to simulate AWS services on their own computers or within continuous integration (CI) environments. Applications communicate with the emulator through a local HTTPS endpoint using the same APIs they would use when connecting to AWS.

Developers can use existing commands to create and manage simulated cloud resources, including Amazon S3 storage buckets and Amazon DynamoDB tables. This allows developers to test supported application workflows without provisioning billable AWS resources.

According to AWS, local API requests can return responses in milliseconds, eliminating the need to wait for cloud resources to be provisioned during supported tests. AWS Emulator has no additional service charge, although testing against actual AWS infrastructure remains subject to standard pricing.

Each emulator instance generates its own credentials and maintains separate resources in memory. This allows developers to run isolated tests within CI environments without sharing simulated resources between test jobs.

Built in Rust, the emulator uses AWS API models to reproduce service behaviour, including expected responses and error messages.

The tool supports local testing workflows involving AI coding agents such as Kiro and Claude Code. These agents can create simulated resources, execute tests, identify errors, and modify application code without repeatedly deploying workloads to AWS.

Advait Patel, senior site reliability engineer at Broadcom, told InfoWorld that local testing reduces the time AI coding agents spend waiting for cloud resources when repeatedly writing, testing, and correcting code.

“Teams get faster feedback, fewer leftover test resources, and smaller dev account bills,” Patel said.

AWS Emulator can be installed through RPM or Debian packages on Linux, while macOS and Windows users can run it through Docker. AWS also provides an embedded mode for the AWS SDK for Rust, allowing tests to run directly within an application process.

How AWS used AI agents to build the emulator

According to Matthew Goldberg, senior principal engineer at AWS, the project began as an experiment using Kiro to generate an implementation of Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS).

Goldberg instructed the coding agent to create tests based on AWS command-line operations, validate them against real AWS services, and develop an in-memory implementation capable of passing those tests. The initial SQS implementation took approximately 15 minutes, although it had limitations.

AWS subsequently generated a web server capable of accepting requests defined by 438 AWS API models. The server initially lacked the underlying service functionality, which autonomous agents were then assigned to develop.

The project eventually developed into a system involving three groups of autonomous AI agents responsible for writing tests, identifying software issues, and implementing fixes. Goldberg said AWS engineers oversee the development system without directly writing or reviewing the emulator’s code.

“Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” Goldberg said in an AWS engineering article.

The first group creates fidelity tests using AWS API models and verifies the results against actual cloud services. According to Goldberg, the system uses tens of thousands of tests to establish expected behaviour and measure how closely the emulator matches AWS.

A second group runs the tests against the emulator and identifies differences between its responses and those of AWS. The findings are recorded as software issues, which are then assigned to a third group of agents responsible for fixing them.

According to Goldberg, hundreds of agents work concurrently on the codebase, resolving thousands of identified issues daily. Each agent working on a fix is assigned a specific issue and must submit its changes for automated review.

The development process has also required adjustments to how the agents write code. Goldberg described an earlier version in which agents attempted to build their own Python interpreter to support AWS Lambda functions, prompting AWS to instruct them to reuse existing software libraries instead.

Each proposed code change must pass automated checks covering compilation, coding standards, security, and compatibility with existing tests. Changes that fail are returned to the agents for revision, while those that pass are merged into the codebase.

AWS said an independent security agent also conducts adversarial reviews while fixes are being developed and again during the release process. These checks are intended to identify security issues in AI-generated code before the changes are published.

The development process uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS CodeCommit, and AWS CodePipeline. Approved changes undergo further building and testing before the software is packaged for release and its source code is published on GitHub.

The public GitHub repository also contains records of software issues identified by the agents, including completed fixes and outstanding problems. AWS maintains separate directories for resolved issues and those awaiting further work.

Testing accuracy and limitations

AWS measures the emulator’s accuracy through fidelity tests comparing API responses, HTTP status codes, error messages, and resulting resource states with actual AWS services. It publishes separate scores for each service, showing how many tests pass out of the total conducted.

These scores can change as additional tests are introduced, even when previously supported operations continue functioning correctly. Operations that have not been implemented return an HTTP 501 (Not Implemented) response.

AWS has published its Emulator Evaluation Suite on GitHub, providing developers with access to the tests used to measure compatibility. According to the repository, each fidelity test has been verified against at least two sandboxed AWS accounts using the AWS SDK for Python.

However, the repository states that behaviour outside the published tests remains unverified. It also includes tests the emulator has not yet passed, allowing developers to examine gaps in compatibility.

AWS’s documentation indicates that the emulator currently matches production services most closely for control-plane operations, including creating, describing, updating, and deleting resources. Support for data-plane operations, such as storing and retrieving data, varies between services.

Compatibility with infrastructure-as-code tools, including AWS CloudFormation, Terraform, and AWS CDK, also varies by service. AWS publishes fidelity scores with each release to document the operations that have been successfully tested.

AWS said the emulator does not evaluate Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies or resource-based permissions in the same way as its production services. Requests rejected by AWS because of insufficient permissions might therefore succeed during local testing.

Each emulator instance also operates as a single simulated AWS account without support for cross-account or cross-Region behaviour.

Devin Pratt, research director at IDC, told InfoWorld that the initial release does not simulate throttling, service outages, snapshot-and-restore operations, or differences in service availability between AWS Regions. Broadcom’s Patel also identified timeouts and partial failures as scenarios that require testing against actual cloud infrastructure to assess application recovery.

Pratt also raised concerns about the emulator’s lack of code isolation. AWS’s security documentation confirms that code executed through the emulator is not sandboxed and can access or modify local files using the developer’s permissions.

AWS said the emulator listens only on the local machine by default and generates its own credentials for API authentication. The company advises developers to run only trusted code and keep real AWS credentials and production data out of the testing environment.

The company advises developers to test security configurations and complete applications in AWS before deploying them to production, rather than relying solely on the emulator.

(Photo by Bernd 📷 Dittrich)

data.title: 9 best cloud browser providers for AI automation
data.description:
Key takeaways

  • Cloud browser platforms provide remote browser environments for AI agents and automation workflows.
  • Providers vary in their support for developer frameworks, managed agent features, and self-hosted deployment.
  • A pilot should measure task success and failure recovery, not just browser startup time.
  • Anchor Browser ranks first for teams that need managed browser execution with authentication and operational controls in the same platform.

AI automation often depends on websites that were built for people, not software agents. An agent may need to sign in, navigate a web app, submit a form, or retrieve information from a dynamic page. A cloud browser provider supplies the remote browser sessions and supporting infrastructure that let an agent perform those tasks without a team operating its own browser fleet.

These providers differ in how they handle authentication, session isolation, debugging, deployment, and scale. Some offer a managed browser API, while others add agent-oriented features or options for self-hosting. The right choice depends on the work your automation performs and how much visibility and control your team needs.

At a glance

  • Anchor Browser: managed sessions with identity and authentication controls
  • Browserbase: browser sessions paired with agent development and replay tools
  • Browserless: framework-compatible browsers with cloud and self-hosted options
  • Kernel: isolated sessions with persistent profiles and managed authentication
  • Browser Use: cloud browsers connected to an open-source agent framework
  • Steel: open-source infrastructure alongside a managed cloud service
  • Bright Data Browser API: browser execution with geographic targeting for data workflows
  • Cloudflare Browser Run: browser tasks integrated with Cloudflare’s developer environment
  • BrowserCat: managed sessions accessed through a single browser API

What cloud browser infrastructure contributes to AI automation

A browser automation library tells a browser what to do. Cloud browser infrastructure provides the environment in which those instructions run. It may create sessions on demand, keep tasks isolated, expose a connection through a familiar protocol, and capture information that helps developers understand a failed run.

The distinction matters because the browser is only one part of an automation stack. Teams may also need an agent framework, application credentials, workflow logic, and a review process. When comparing providers, consider:

  • Execution: Which browser engines, protocols, and automation frameworks can connect?
  • State and access: How are cookies, profiles, credentials, and network settings managed?
  • Operations: Can teams inspect sessions, run work concurrently, and recover from failures?

9 cloud browser providers for AI automation

Anchor browser: Managed cloud browsers for AI automation

Anchor Browser provides managed cloud browser sessions for agents and automation workflows. Developers can connect through APIs, SDKs, MCP, or browser automation tools, allowing agents to interact with web applications through the browser rather than relying only on application APIs.

The platform’s emphasis on authenticated workflows is relevant when an agent must work inside a logged-in application. Teams can configure identities and authentication flows for sessions, while controls such as isolation, recordings, and live session visibility help operators monitor execution. Anchor Browser also supports options for network configuration and deployment, which organisations can evaluate against their security and data requirements.

Anchor Browser ranks first because its scope connects browser execution with several operational needs teams encounter when moving automation beyond a prototype: identity, session management, monitoring, and integration with agent workflows. It is not a substitute for defining what an agent is authorised to do. Teams still need to scope permissions and decide which actions require review.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Managed Chromium sessions accessible through APIs and integrations
  • Authentication and identity management for browser tasks
  • Session visibility and recordings for troubleshooting
  • Deployment and network options to assess for enterprise requirements

Browserbase: Hosted sessions with developer inspection tools

Browserbase provides cloud-hosted browser sessions that developers can control through common automation tools. Its platform also includes Stagehand, an open-source SDK for building browser agents, with tools for actions, observations, and structured extraction. Teams can use Browserbase sessions independently or pair them with Stagehand.

For operational debugging, Browserbase offers session observability features such as live views, logs, and replays. These can help developers see how an agent interacted with a page and investigate where a task went wrong. Browserbase also offers options for running agent code close to browser sessions, which may simplify deployment for certain workloads.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Hosted browser sessions and common automation integrations
  • Stagehand SDK for browser agent development
  • Live views, logs, and session replay
  • Options for deploying agent code near browser sessions

Browserless: Managed or self-hosted browser capacity

Browserless provides managed headless browsers for automation. Developers can connect using Puppeteer or Playwright over WebSocket, or use APIs for tasks such as screenshots, PDFs, and page extraction. Browserless also supports running its infrastructure in the cloud or self-hosting with Docker.

This range of connection options can help teams adapt existing browser scripts without rebuilding their automation around a proprietary interface. Browserless also supports browser sessions that stay open across multi-step workflows, and its platform documentation describes how to connect an LLM-driven agent to a browser.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Managed Chromium and other browser instances
  • Puppeteer and Playwright connections
  • REST and GraphQL APIs for browser tasks
  • Cloud service or Docker-based self-hosting

Kernel: Isolated sessions and persistent browser state

Kernel offers sandboxed, cloud-hosted Chromium sessions for agents that need to interact with websites. Developers can connect through browser automation protocols and SDKs, or use computer-control features for agents that work from screenshots and visual input.

Kernel ranks fourth because it brings session isolation and persistent state into the centre of its infrastructure offering. That can matter when an agent’s task spans multiple pages or sessions and needs a consistent browser context. Teams should test the startup characteristics, session duration limits, authentication flow, and cost profile using their own workloads rather than relying on general benchmarks.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Sandboxed cloud Chromium sessions
  • Browser profiles and managed authentication
  • Live views, recordings, logs, and telemetry
  • Browser pools and on-demand session options

Browser use: Cloud browsers alongside an agent framework

Browser Use combines an open-source browser agent framework with cloud browser infrastructure. Teams can use its framework to build agent behaviour or connect their own agents and automation scripts to its hosted browser environment. This means it can address both the browser runtime and some of the logic used to operate it.

The platform supports connections through familiar browser automation interfaces, making it possible to test cloud sessions with an existing workflow. Browser Use also promotes handling of sites that restrict automated access. As with any provider making access-related claims, teams should validate those results on the specific websites and use cases they are authorised to automate.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Open-source browser agent framework
  • Hosted browser infrastructure
  • Connections for custom agents and automation scripts
  • Browser interactions intended for dynamic web tasks

Steel: Open-source browser infrastructure with a managed option

Steel provides cloud browser infrastructure for AI agents, with an open-source browser server that teams can host themselves and a managed cloud service. It supports connections through standard browser automation protocols and tools, including Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium.

The managed service adds features such as session persistence, proxy support, and CAPTCHA handling. Teams can use Steel’s APIs and SDKs to create and control sessions, while its documentation includes integrations for several agent frameworks and computer-use workflows. The self-hosted option gives infrastructure teams more control over where browser workloads run, but also means they own deployment and maintenance.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Open-source browser server for self-hosting
  • Managed cloud browser sessions
  • Compatibility with common browser automation frameworks
  • Session persistence and network-related features

Bright data browser API: Browser sessions for data-intensive workflows

Bright Data’s Browser API provides hosted browsers for dynamic web data collection and automation. It supports scripts built with Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium, and offers proxy management and CAPTCHA-solving capabilities as part of its browser service.

The product is oriented toward workflows where pages need to be rendered and interacted with before data can be collected. It includes geographic and ASN targeting, autoscaling infrastructure, and real-time monitoring options. These features can be relevant to AI automation pipelines that need to gather information from JavaScript-heavy pages and pass the results to another system.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Hosted browsers for Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium
  • JavaScript rendering and browser-based data collection
  • Geographic and ASN targeting
  • Autoscaling and monitoring features

Cloudflare browser run: Browser sessions within the Cloudflare environment

Cloudflare Browser Run, formerly Browser Rendering, lets developers control headless browser instances on Cloudflare’s network. It supports browser tasks such as screenshots, PDFs, scraping, and page interaction. Developers can use quick actions for stateless tasks or control sessions through Puppeteer, Playwright, CDP, or Stagehand.

The product is particularly connected to Cloudflare Workers: developers can deploy browser workflows in that environment or connect to sessions from elsewhere using CDP. This may simplify architecture for teams already running application logic on Cloudflare. It also offers a browser API for tasks that do not require a long-lived interactive session.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Headless browser access on Cloudflare’s network
  • Quick actions for screenshots, PDFs, and scraping
  • Playwright, Puppeteer, CDP, and Stagehand sessions
  • Integration with Cloudflare Workers

Browsercat: A single API for managed browser sessions

BrowserCat provides an API for connecting to managed cloud browsers. Developers can use a WebSocket connection with Playwright- or CDP-compatible clients, while BrowserCat manages the browser backend. The platform describes support for running multiple parallel browsers and using a consistent endpoint as its backend infrastructure evolves.

This model can reduce the amount of browser infrastructure a team has to operate directly. It is applicable to workflows such as browser automation, testing, scraping, and agent-driven web interactions. Teams should review how BrowserCat’s API maps to their chosen automation framework and whether the available browser configuration meets the needs of their tasks.

Relevant capabilities include:

  • Managed cloud browser sessions
  • WebSocket connection for Playwright- and CDP-compatible clients
  • Parallel browser execution
  • A single API endpoint for browser access

Match the provider to the automation workload

Provider comparisons become more useful when based on the workflow rather than a generic feature checklist. A data extraction task may depend on rendering and network configuration, while an agent handling an internal SaaS workflow may need a persistent identity and a reviewable session.

  • For signed-in business applications: test login continuity, identity scoping, session expiration, and human intervention.
  • For high-volume execution: measure concurrency, browser startup, queueing, retries, and cleanup under realistic load.
  • For troubleshooting: check whether the platform captures logs, screenshots, recordings, or network events.
  • For deployment planning: compare managed cloud, private deployment, and self-hosted options.

What to test before moving browser agents into production

A short pilot can reveal operational gaps that a feature list may not show. Choose one repeatable task and test it across normal and failure conditions. Keep the task within the access permissions granted by the website or application owner.

  • Repeatability: Run the same task with different page states and confirm the output remains verifiable.
  • Authentication: Test expected login, session expiration, and re-authentication paths without exposing credentials to the agent.
  • Failure recovery: Introduce a timeout or changed page element and check how the workflow reports or recovers.
  • Concurrency: Increase parallel sessions gradually and observe latency, queueing, and resource behaviour.
  • Auditability: Confirm that the team can determine what the browser did, which identity it used, and what data it accessed.

Frequently asked questions

What is a cloud browser provider?

A cloud browser provider runs browser sessions remotely and makes them available through an API or browser automation protocol. The provider typically manages browser startup and some combination of isolation, scaling, networking, and session monitoring. Teams connect their own scripts or agents to those sessions, although some providers also offer agent frameworks or workflow tools.

Why do AI automation workflows use cloud browsers?

Cloud browsers give AI agents a remote environment to interact with web applications and dynamic pages. They can support tasks such as navigation, form entry, page inspection, and file handling when an appropriate API is unavailable. Remote execution also lets teams run sessions independently of a developer’s computer, though the provider’s security and session controls still need evaluation.

What should teams compare when evaluating providers?

data.title: Cloud security questions for accounting firms moving data
data.description:
A practice manager at a 20-person accounting firm in Leeds is comparing three cloud platforms. She sends each vendor the same first question: “Is our data encrypted?”

All three say yes. Within the hour, in fact, with nicely formatted answers. She’s no closer to a decision than she was that morning.

That’s the trouble with the question most firms ask first. Encryption at rest and in transit is the baseline now, and any vendor that can’t say yes probably shouldn’t be on your shortlist anyway. The questions that actually separate a sensible choice from a risky one are less comfortable to ask. They’re about where the data sits, what the vendor can prove, who can get in, what happens when things break, and how you’d ever leave.

Accounting firms have more reason than most to ask them properly. They hold National Insurance numbers, bank details, payroll records, and years of financial history for every client. And under UK GDPR, the firm is still the data controller when a vendor stores that information. You can move the data to the cloud. You can’t move the responsibility.

Here are the questions worth putting to any vendor before you sign, and what a good answer sounds like.

Where does our data actually live, and who else can reach IT?

Start with geography, because it shapes almost everything else. Ask which country, and ideally which data centre region, will store your client files and backups. If any of it leaves the UK, you need to know where it goes and what legal safeguards cover the transfer. Readers who’ve followed the recent sovereign cloud debates will recognise the underlying worry: data stored under another country’s jurisdiction can be subject to that country’s rules.

Then ask the question most firms skip: who are your subprocessors? Almost every cloud product is built on other cloud products. Your practice software might run on a hyperscaler, send emails through one provider, process e-signatures through another, and run AI features through a third. Each of those companies may touch your clients’ data.

A trustworthy vendor will send you a current subprocessor list without fuss and tell you how they notify customers when it changes. Honestly, that list is often the most revealing document in the whole evaluation. A vendor that can’t produce one, or takes three weeks to find it, is telling you something about how closely they track their own supply chain.

Can you prove IT, beyond a badge on your website?

Knowing where your data lives is only useful if you can trust what happens to it there. That’s where certifications come in, and where a lot of firms take a logo at face value.

Let’s break down the three you’re most likely to see, because they measure quite different things.

SOC 2 Type II is the one most worth asking about. It’s an independent auditor’s report on whether a company’s security controls actually worked over a stretch of time, usually six to twelve months. Watch out for the Type I version, which only confirms the controls existed on a single day. That’s a bit like judging a restaurant’s hygiene on the morning of a scheduled inspection.

ISO 27001 tells you something broader: that the company runs a formal information security management system and keeps reviewing it. And Cyber Essentials, the UK government-backed scheme, covers the technical basics like firewalls and patching. If a vendor holds Cyber Essentials Plus, an assessor has actually tested those controls rather than taking the company’s word for it.

The practical move is to ask for the report or certificate itself, not the marketing page about it. Then check two things: the date, and the scope. A certification that covers the vendor’s corporate IT but not the product you’re actually buying won’t do you much good. Most vendors will share a SOC 2 report under an NDA. If one won’t, ask yourself why.

Who on our team can see what?

So far, every question has been about the vendor. This one is about you, and it’s where a surprising number of real incidents start.

Picture a seasonal contractor who helps out during the January self-assessment rush. She leaves at the end of February. In June, someone notices her login still works, and it can see every client the firm has. Nobody was careless, exactly. The firm just never had a process for turning access off, and the software didn’t make it obvious.

Here’s how to make this part of the evaluation work for you: sit down with your actual staff list and test each platform’s permissions against it. Could the junior bookkeeper be limited to the dozen clients she really works on? Payroll data should be kept separate from tax files, too. Multi-factor authentication needs to be something you can enforce for everyone, rather than switch on for yourself and hope the rest of the team follows. And if something does go wrong, you’ll be very glad of an audit log showing who opened which file, and when.

The right answers here depend partly on how your firm is organised. But a platform that only offers “admin” and “user” roles will force you into giving people more access than they need, and that’s a risk you’ll carry every day.

How do clients actually get documents to US?

Internal access is one half of the picture. The other half sits outside the firm entirely, with clients, and it’s the weak link most security reviews never get round to.

You can choose the most secure platform on the market and still have a client email a scanned passport, three P60s, and a bank statement as plain attachments, copied to her husband’s work address for good measure. Clients don’t do this because they’re careless. They do it because email is easy and nobody gave them a better option that felt just as simple.

So ask vendors what the client’s side looks like. Is there a secure portal or app where clients can upload files and sign documents? Can clients use it from a phone without calling your office for help? And, crucially, does the platform actively steer clients towards it?

That last point is where security and workflow overlap. If document requests, reminders, and status updates all run through the same system, clients get used to uploading there instead of replying by email. The TaxDome workflow tool is one example of this approach: each job moves through a set pipeline, and the platform sends automated requests and reminders that point clients to its secure portal, which sits on a SOC 2 Type II certified platform with role-based access and two-factor authentication. Whichever product you pick, the test is simple. Would a busy client choose the secure route without being told twice?

What happens on your worst day?

Everything above is about keeping problems out. This question is about what happens when one gets in anyway, or when the service simply stops working.

Outages first. CloudTech readers will remember the recent Google Cloud outage that disrupted several UK banks. If the biggest providers can go down, so can the smaller platforms built on top of them. Ask how often the vendor backs up your data, how long a full restore would take, and whether they’ve ever actually tested one. Then think about timing. An outage in August is an inconvenience. An outage in the last week of January, with the self-assessment deadline days away, is a very different conversation with your clients.

Breaches are where the legal detail matters. Under UK GDPR, your firm, as the controller, generally has 72 hours from becoming aware of a reportable breach to notify the ICO. Your vendor, as a processor, has to tell you “without undue delay”, but the law doesn’t set a fixed number of hours for that step. So the speed of your own response depends heavily on what your contract says. Ask for a specific notification window in writing.

One more tip that tends to cut through the polished answers: ask the vendor to walk you through their last real incident. Not the policy document, the actual event. What went wrong, how fast they spotted it, and what they changed afterwards. A vendor that has never had an incident to talk about is either very new or not being entirely open.

What does your AI do with our clients’ data?

A couple of years ago, this question wouldn’t have made the list. Now nearly every practice platform has added AI features that read documents, draft emails, or summarise client files, and each one raises a few new things to check.

I’d start with the question clients are now asking firms directly: is their data ever used to train the vendor’s models, or anyone else’s? A clear “no” written into the contract, not just mentioned in an FAQ, is what you want to hear. It’s also worth knowing whether you can switch AI features off, either firm-wide or for the one client who’d rather you didn’t. Then find out where the processing happens. An AI feature that sends documents to an outside model provider has quietly added another name to your subprocessor list, which takes us right back to the first question.

None of this means avoiding AI. Plenty of these features save real hours during busy season. It just means treating them like any other part of the system that touches client data, with the same scrutiny and the same paperwork.

If we leave, what do we take with US?

It feels odd to plan a break-up before the relationship has started. But this is the question that protects you if any of the earlier answers turn out to be wrong.

Ask how you’d export your data, and in what format. A neat archive of PDFs is fine for storage, but it won’t help much if you need to move years of client records, notes, and task history into a new system. Ask how long the vendor keeps your data after you cancel, and whether they’ll confirm deletion in writing once it’s gone, including from backups.

It’s also worth thinking about records you’re obliged to keep. Accounting firms generally hold onto client records for years after an engagement ends, so you need to be sure you’ll still have them, in a usable form, long after you’ve stopped paying for the platform that created them.

The best time to negotiate any of this is before you sign. Once three years of client data is sitting in someone else’s system, you’ll have far less use.

data.title: Anthropic expands Microsoft cloud deal by up to $4.3 billion
data.description:
Anthropic has increased its cloud computing commitments with Microsoft by up to $4.3 billion, bringing the total value of its agreement to between $47.2 billion and $49.2 billion.

The revised figures were disclosed in an updated IPO filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 10, 2026. The agreement covers computing services between November 2026 and June 2033, regardless of how much capacity Anthropic uses.

The previous filing, dated November 2, listed a minimum spending commitment of $44.9 billion. The latest amendment raises the minimum commitment by $2.3 billion to $47.2 billion, with an additional $2 billion bringing the maximum to $49.2 billion.

Anthropic originally signed the Microsoft agreement in November 2025 and subsequently amended it several times between February and November 2026. The commitment cannot be cancelled except in cases involving Microsoft’s unresolved material breach or certain computing capacity that has not been delivered.

Anthropic said it typically reserves computing capacity 12 to 18 months before deployment. The company said comparable short-term computing resources currently cost substantially more than capacity secured through multi-year agreements, which generally involve fixed near-term expenses.

Anthropic’s cloud infrastructure agreements

Microsoft is one of several infrastructure providers supporting Anthropic’s AI computing requirements. The company also has long-term agreements with Google and Amazon, alongside arrangements with specialist infrastructure providers.

Under its agreement with Google, Anthropic has committed to spending at least $121.3 billion on cloud hosting services between April 2026 and July 2033. It also plans to procure additional Google Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) capacity between 2028 and 2031, with estimated future payments ranging from $125 billion to $150 billion.

The additional TPU capacity can be obtained through Google Cloud, direct hardware purchases, or third-party providers. These estimated payments are separate from the fixed contractual obligations disclosed in Anthropic’s financial statements.

Anthropic also has a minimum spending commitment of $110 billion with Amazon between May 2026 and April 2036. Its agreements with Microsoft, Google, and Amazon generally require minimum payments regardless of actual computing usage, subject to specified contractual exceptions.

Anthropic has also secured Nvidia GPU capacity through agreements with specialist infrastructure providers, including SpaceXAI and Nscale. The agreements carry maximum spending commitments of $120.5 billion and approximately $44.6 billion, respectively.

Unlike its hyperscaler agreements, some of Anthropic’s specialist infrastructure contracts tie payments to the delivery and acceptance of computing capacity. The arrangements also contain different conditions governing service availability, delivery milestones, and termination rights.

Lambda agreement and Anthropic’s direct infrastructure plans

The updated filing also disclosed a contractual development involving Lambda, another provider of Nvidia-powered cloud computing infrastructure.

Anthropic entered into three agreements with Lambda in May, June, and August 2026, covering approximately $41.3 billion in computing services through 2034. Payments under these agreements are tied to capacity delivered to and accepted by Anthropic.

The August agreement accounts for approximately $34.9 billion of the total commitment. Under its terms, either party can terminate the contract if Lambda fails to secure a required facility lease by an agreed deadline.

According to the filing, Lambda did not secure the lease before the deadline, making the August agreement eligible for termination by either party.

However, neither company had issued a termination notice as of November 10. “We do not currently intend to terminate the agreement,” Anthropic said in the filing.

Anthropic is also expanding its computing arrangements beyond cloud service agreements through a direct infrastructure procurement model known as Anthropic Direct. The approach involves leasing computing hardware and hosting it in dedicated data centres operated by third parties.

The model separates commitments for data centre capacity from the hardware deployed inside those facilities. According to Anthropic, data centres generally require longer development lead times but account for a smaller portion of total computing infrastructure costs.

By separating the two commitments, Anthropic can secure data centre space earlier while deferring larger accelerator investments until its computing requirements are clearer. Its first facility under the model became operational in 2026.

Anthropic said the model combines its existing cloud agreements with directly leased infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on fixed-term cloud contracts. It expects Anthropic Direct to account for a growing share of its computing investments over time.

Computing expenses and future commitments

Anthropic’s compute and infrastructure expenses increased from $944 million in the first quarter of 2025 to $9.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, according to its filing. The company attributed the increase to the delivery of computing capacity under previously signed multi-year agreements.

During the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic recorded $18.8 billion in compute and infrastructure expenses, compared with $4.4 billion during the same period in 2025. Of the 2026 total, approximately $6.5 billion related to short-term computing commitments, which the company said cost substantially more than comparable multi-year arrangements.

Anthropic also disclosed that its computing requirements have previously exceeded forecasts, limiting capacity available for certain product development and deployment activities. Its infrastructure expenses are generally fixed in the near term, while much of its revenue depends on customer consumption.

Anthropic’s latest filing puts its aggregate spending commitments at approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which relates to computing infrastructure. The total increased from approximately $895.4 billion disclosed in its November 2 filing and represents contractual obligations rather than expenses already incurred.

The commitments include future purchases, short-term agreements, and leases that have not yet commenced. Anthropic estimates that approximately $451.6 billion will be incurred by the end of 2030, with the remaining commitments largely scheduled between 2031 and 2045.

The $900.9 billion figure excludes an estimated $150 billion to $175 billion in payments under computing and infrastructure agreements without fixed dollar commitments. Anthropic said the actual amounts will depend on capacity delivered and deployed, delivery schedules, pricing arrangements, and whether specified contractual conditions are met or waived.

data.title: Railway breach exposes AI credentials, triggers $740,000 in charges
data.description:
Cloud hosting provider Railway has disclosed that attackers exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure to steal customer credentials, resulting in approximately US$740,000 in unauthorised AI usage. The incident potentially exposed environment variables belonging to no more than 1.85% of its workspaces, or approximately 100,000.

In an incident report, Railway said the attackers gained access to its internal source code and decrypted some customer environment variables during an intrusion on October 20 and 21. The company said its forensic logs established the maximum number of workspaces whose variables could have been decrypted, but not the exact number of individual credentials exposed.

Railway’s investigation found that the attackers primarily targeted AI provider credentials. Some searches also involved cloud, database, and payment service credentials, but the company found no evidence that customer databases were accessed.

How attackers accessed Railway’s cloud infrastructure

The attack began on October 20 when the threat actor exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. The flaw allowed the attacker to partially bypass filesystem isolation and obtain an internal credential used by build servers to communicate with other systems.

The stolen credential allowed the attacker to access Railway’s internal build management system and retrieve build histories and source code. The attacker then exploited a misconfigured OpenID Connect (OIDC) trust relationship to obtain temporary cloud credentials and access additional infrastructure.

Using those credentials, the attacker accessed a machine responsible for infrastructure orchestration. The machine contained a longer-lived credential that allowed the attacker to retrieve and decrypt customer environment variables stored in Railway’s production database.

Railway protected these variables using envelope encryption, with separate encryption keys for each environment. However, the stolen credential allowed the attacker to request decryption through Railway’s key management service without directly accessing the root encryption key.

Railway’s logs showed that the attacker specifically searched for variable names associated with AI provider keys. The attacker also prioritised environments containing large numbers of stored variables.

Between October 20 and 21, the attacker accessed the histories of 353 builds and decrypted variables from a subset of customer environments. Railway said it found no indication that the attacker downloaded customer Git repositories.

Stolen AI credentials lead to unauthorised charges

Railway said it is coordinating with affected AI service providers to secure refunds for unauthorised usage. The company has committed to covering charges that providers decline to reimburse.

According to Railway, reimbursement arrangements vary between providers. AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini have initiated refunds under their existing fraud policies, while OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing affected claims individually.

Anthropic-related charges remain under discussion, with Railway covering the costs in the meantime. OpenRouter has maintained its no-refund policy, leaving Railway to cover the associated unauthorised charges.

The compromised information also included linked-account tokens belonging to 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and AI agent keys. Railway said it reset those tokens, notified affected users, and found no evidence of attackers using the stolen credentials to log into Railway accounts.

Railway’s investigation also examined how the stolen credentials were used. “Our internal forensic investigation suggests AI provider keys were the primary target of the attack,” Railway said in its incident report.

The company believes the credentials were passed to intermediary services for use in model distillation, although it has not established whether the original attacker operated those services. Observed unauthorised usage included coding-agent requests and AI training workloads.

Separate research from cybersecurity company Wiz provides further details about the misuse of stolen AI credentials. In its Black October investigation, Wiz documented cases of attackers accessing paid AI models without authorisation, a practice known as LLMjacking.

The researchers examined two compromised AWS Bedrock credentials associated with an unnamed affected vendor. Attackers generated approximately 800,000 API calls over 30 hours using one credential and 1.7 million calls over 13 hours using the other.

Wiz estimated that the combined usage exceeded US$100,000 at list prices. Researchers also identified infrastructure associated with AI model resale services that had tested the compromised credentials, although they could not establish whether those operators were responsible for the original breaches or subsequent unauthorised usage.

The Wall Street Journal reported on November 11 that stolen AI computing access was being sold through intermediary services offering discounted access to AI models. The reporting described a market in which stolen credentials can be used to obtain computing resources without paying the original service providers.

Another cloud development platform, Zeabur, suffered a separate breach in October that resulted in approximately US$100,000 in fraudulent charges, according to The Wall Street Journal. In its October 19 incident report, Zeabur said attackers used leaked internal credentials to access its cloud infrastructure and retrieve environment variables stored in its platform database.

Zeabur’s investigation identified several security weaknesses, including overly broad permissions and long-lived administrative credentials stored in plaintext. The company subsequently revoked compromised credentials and restricted access to affected systems.

In an October 28 follow-up statement, Zeabur said, “Under our current financial circumstances, we are unable to pay for third-party service charges arising from the October 2026 security incident.”

The company offered to help affected customers request refunds or fee waivers from their service providers. It also announced that it would cease operations on December 31, 2026.

Railway strengthens cloud security following the breach

Railway said it removed the attacker from its systems on October 21 and disabled the compromised credentials. During its response, the company temporarily suspended builds, invalidated user sessions, and worked with providers including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and GitHub to revoke potentially exposed keys.

The response also affected customers attempting to replace compromised credentials. Railway said the resulting increase in build activity contributed to demand reaching nearly two orders of magnitude above its normal baseline, adding pressure to its infrastructure.

At the same time, Railway accelerated its migration to a new build system designed to improve workload isolation. The rollout required additional computing and storage capacity, contributing to delays in restoring build functionality.

The disruption left some customers unable to redeploy applications with replacement credentials until builds resumed. Railway acknowledged that some customers experienced downtime during the recovery process.

Build functionality was restored across all subscription plans by October 22. Railway also accelerated the deployment of a new build system that assigns each build a dedicated temporary virtual machine, adding another layer of isolation between workloads.

Under the revised architecture, each build receives a temporary credential restricted to pushing a specific container image. Railway has also centralised encryption and decryption logging and limited access to customer secrets to authorised services.

The company said it has remediated all identified vulnerabilities exploited during the incident and introduced additional restrictions on internal credentials. Railway has also engaged an external forensic specialist to continue investigating the breach.

(Photo by Zulfugar Karimov)

data.title: Amazon discloses $80 billion loan facility as AI infrastructure spending rises
data.description:
Amazon has disclosed a new loan facility that allows it to borrow up to $80 billion to purchase technology infrastructure assets. The financing arrangement comes as the company increases spending on cloud computing and AI infrastructure.

According to Amazon’s third-quarter filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the facility forms part of its supplier financing arrangements for technology infrastructure purchases. The company can access the funds at its discretion between the first quarter of 2027 and the third quarter of 2028.

The amount available will depend on the timing and extent of purchase orders, as well as pricing terms. Borrowings will carry variable interest rates and mature five years after each withdrawal.

Amazon will provide security interests in certain assets purchased through the facility, with outstanding borrowings recorded as long-term debt on its balance sheet. The filing does not specify which infrastructure assets will be purchased or identify the lenders involved.

The facility provides for potential borrowings of up to approximately $80 billion rather than funds Amazon has already drawn.

Amazon’s infrastructure spending

Amazon’s latest financial results also showed higher capital expenditure, primarily driven by investments in technology infrastructure.

Amazon reported cash capital expenditure of $75.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, compared with $34.2 billion during the same period last year. Spending for the first nine months of 2026 reached $172.2 billion, up from $89.9 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The company said the expenditure primarily reflected investments in technology infrastructure, most of which supported the growth of AWS, alongside additional capacity for its fulfilment network.

Amazon expects cash capital expenditure to reach approximately $220 billion for the full year. It also expects spending to increase further in 2027, primarily because of continued investments in technology infrastructure.

The increase is reflected in AWS’s infrastructure assets. According to Amazon’s SEC filing, the cloud division’s net property and equipment assets rose from $190.1 billion at the end of 2025 to $313 billion as of September 30, 2026.

AWS recorded $147.2 billion in net additions to property and equipment during the first nine months of 2026, compared with $64.8 billion a year earlier. The figures include non-cash activity, such as equipment acquired but not yet paid for, and are not equivalent to cash capital expenditure.

Amazon’s infrastructure costs include servers, networking equipment, data centre depreciation and amortisation, rent, and utilities associated with AWS and other Amazon businesses. The company said higher infrastructure spending, including depreciation and amortisation, was the main reason technology and infrastructure costs increased during the quarter.

AWS’s depreciation and amortisation expenses reached $9.23 billion in the third quarter, up from $5.65 billion a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, these expenses increased to $24.6 billion from $14.9 billion in the corresponding period last year.

Amazon also reported approximately $883.6 billion in contractual commitments as of September 30, 2026. These included $159.6 billion in property and equipment commitments and $164.9 billion in leases that had not yet commenced.

These commitments cover multiple years and business activities, not just AWS. Amazon’s filing also disclosed purchasing arrangements that allow the company to defer payments for certain technology infrastructure assets for up to one year.

Higher capital expenditure has also affected Amazon’s cash flow. The company reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, compared with positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion a year earlier.

Amazon attributed the decline primarily to a $94.8 billion year-on-year increase in purchases of property and equipment, net of proceeds from sales and incentives, mainly related to AI investments.

AWS growth and financing

AWS reported revenue of $46 billion in the third quarter of 2026, an increase of 39.3% from the previous year. According to Amazon, this was the cloud division’s fastest revenue growth in nearly five years.

Operating income for AWS increased to $17.8 billion from $11.4 billion a year earlier. Amazon attributed the revenue increase primarily to higher customer usage, partially offset by pricing changes associated with long-term customer contracts.

During Amazon’s third-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy discussed the pace of the company’s AI infrastructure deployment.

“We’re installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds,” Jassy said, adding that customers were using the new capacity almost as quickly as AWS installed it.

Jassy also reported that Amazon’s chip business continued to record triple-digit year-on-year percentage growth, while revenue commitments for its Graviton processors and Trainium AI accelerators had each increased more than twentyfold.

“Our Chips business continues to grow triple digit percentages year over year,” Jassy said during the earnings call.

Amazon has not specified whether its custom AI accelerators will be financed through the new $80 billion facility.

Amazon has also secured financing through other borrowing arrangements in 2026. These include a $17.5 billion unsecured term loan agreed in June and drawn in September, alongside bond issuances denominated in US dollars and several other currencies.

The new $80 billion facility differs from these unsecured borrowing arrangements because Amazon will provide security interests in certain infrastructure assets purchased through it.

As of September 30, 2026, Amazon reported $173.1 billion in long-term debt on its balance sheet, compared with $65.6 billion at the end of 2025.
